name: Eyelash perm (Lash perm)

card.summary: A salon treatment that chemically curls natural lashes for a semi-permanent lifted, more open-eyed look.
card.note: Chemicals near the eye can cause irritation; clinicians advise professional application only.

quick.overview:
An eyelash perm uses perming chemistry to curl natural lashes upward, so the eyes look more open and the lashes appear longer without mascara or a curler. Results last until the lashes grow out, about two to three months.

Wikipedia describes the process as taking about 30 to 45 minutes. Medical sources focus on risks, noting limited research on long-term effects.
quick.how: A technician attaches the lashes to a rod or silicone pad, applies a perm solution for 10 to 15 minutes, then a neutralizer for a similar time. Treatments are repeated every few months.
quick.risks: Cleveland Clinic lists allergic reactions, over-processing, possible eyelid inflammation and unknown long-term effects, and says not to do it at home. Ophthalmologists quoted in the press warn that perm solution in the eye can injure the cornea.

lead: An eyelash perm, also called a lash lift, is a cosmetic salon procedure that curls natural eyelashes using hair-perming technology.[1][2] The curled lashes make eyes look more open, and the effect lasts until the lashes are replaced.[2]

Wikipedia describes the process as gluing lashes to a rod or pad, applying perm solution and neutralizer, taking 30 to 45 minutes, with results lasting two to three months.[1] Cleveland Clinic notes it does not make lashes longer or thicker.[2]
Medical commentary highlights allergic reactions, eyelid inflammation and damage from over-processing, and notes limited research on long-term effects.[2]

chain: Lashes bound to a rod and chemically reshaped
Eyes appear more open, lashes look longer
angle.text: The treatment gives a lasting curl without daily curling, adding lift to the lash line for roughly the duration of the lash cycle.

paras: The perm breaks and reforms the protein bonds of the lash, setting a curl; some systems finish with a nourishing oil that also loosens the glue.[1] Before perming, people relied on lash curlers and mascara; Kurlash made the first eyelash curler, and an early human curling method was developed by Charles Nessler in 1905. Perming became widely available after about 2000.[1]

Cleveland Clinic lists allergic reactions (redness, swelling, rash), overprocessing, a possible increase in blepharitis risk, and limited long-term research; it advises professional application, a patch test and occasional use.[2] Wikipedia notes the FDA has approved hair treatments but not this procedure for use around the eyes.[1]

timeline.event: Charles Nessler develops an early lash curling method.[1]
